Before observing the characteristics of a resonant series circuit, there are two points to bring out.
1) Effect of low impedance on test equipment.
2) Resistance of the coil in an inductor.
The first point, effect of low impedance on test equipment, may reduce the output voltage of the function generator. This effect is easily seen using the oscilloscope.
LOW IMPEDANCE AT RESONANCE - At resonance, XL and XC cancel leaving only the value of R as the impedance. For circuit A at resonance impedance equals 100 W.
1. Set the frequency of the function generator to 10 kHz.
2. Ensure switch S1 on PC130-18A is set to the right.
3. Connect the oscilloscope to TP14 on PC130-18A...
MEASUREMENT SETUP - S1 to the right (power applied) CH1 probe to TP14.
MEASUREMENT SETUP - Frequency - 1
Range - 10 k Output - 5 Vpp
4. Adjust the output voltage of the function generator to 5 Vpp.
5. Slowly increase the frequency of the function generator from 10 kHz to 90 kHz and observe the amplitude of the output signal on the oscilloscope. Adjust the TIME/DIV control as necessary.
If the type of function generator you are using is sensitive to low impedance, you will notice that the output voltage of the generator is lower between 40 and 50 kHz.
The effect is due to the output impedance of the function generator, normally 50 W, supplying voltage to a 100 W circuit that is at resonance.

The second point, resistance of the coil in an inductor, causes the voltage drop across the series resistor NOT to EQUAL the applied voltage at resonance. This is also easily seen on the oscilloscope...
1. Set the output frequency of the function generator to resonance for circuit A, 50.4 kHz.
2. Ensure that the CH1 probe of the oscilloscope is still connected to TP14 on PC130-18A.
3. Adjust the output voltage of the function generator to 5 Vpp.
MEASUREMENT SETUP - S1 to the right (power applied) CH1 probe to TP14
MEASUREMENT SETUP - Frequency - 5.4
Range - 10 k Output - 5 Vpp

4. Connect the CH1 probe to TP4 on PC130-18A. This measures the voltage drop across R1. Notice that the peak to peak voltage measurement is not 5 V as it should be for a LCR series resonant circuit....
MEASUREMENT SETUP - CH1 probe to TP4.
The effect is due to the construction of inductors, the wire coil has resistance. This resistance is like a resistors resistance, it does not change with frequency.
The resistance of inductors is small, between 10 to 150 W. However, compared to R1 at 100 W, the effect of the coil resistance is seen at resonance.
In both effects, if the resistance of R1 is increased, say to 2 kW, the effects of low impedance on test equipment and on R1's voltage drop is reduced.
Keeping these two points in mind, let's observe the characteristics of a series resonant circuit. Let's first look at voltage magnification.

Also notice that the voltage is a little higher across the inductor (at resonance, El and Ec should be equal). The difference is due to the voltage drop of the coil.
The reason El and Ec exceed Ea is because in the first half cycle, the magnetic field of the inductor stores the energy of the discharging capacitor, which adds to Ea.
In the second half cycle, the stored energy in the inductor charges the capacitor, this again adds to Ea. Because of this, both El and Ec are Higher than Ea.

7. Lower frequency of the function generator to 30 kHz. Check Ea at TP14. Notice Er1 is approximately .6 Vpp.
8. Raise frequency of the function generator to 70 kHz. Check Ea at TP14. Notice Er1 is approximately .9 Vpp.
9. Lower frequency of the function generator to 20 kHz. Check Ea at TP14. Notice Er1 is approximately .3Vpp.
10. Raise frequency of the function generator to 80 kHz. Check Ea at TP14. Notice Er1 is approximately .7 Vpp....

Connecting the dots graphically illustrates that the voltage drop across R is maximum at resonance.
Total circuit current can also be illustrated by a graph. Remember, current is the same in all points in a series circuit.
The current through R1 equals the voltage across R1 divided by the resistance. Dividing Er1 by 100 gives total current.
The graph vividly illustrates that total current is maximum at resonance.
Total circuit impedance can also be illustrated by a graph. Remember Zt equals Ea divided by It.
Dividing total current (from the current graph) into 5 Vpp gives total impedance.
The graph graphically illustrates that total impedance is minimum at resonance.
These graphs are important and will be used again in your studies of circuits called reactive filters.
